How Streaming Split
the Billboard Hot 100
in Two

Over 67 years of the pop charts, the typical song's life has collapsed — while a handful of hits linger longer than ever.

1958197019801990200020102025

For more than sixty years, the Billboard Hot 100 has been American pop music’s official scoreboard. Every week it ranks the country’s 100 most popular songs, and for most of that time the recipe was simple: radio play and record sales. Landing on it meant you had a hit. Climbing it meant you were a star. Today the chart counts streams too, and that quiet change turns out to matter more than anyone expected.

One song just would not leave. “Lose Control,” by Teddy Swims, sat on the Hot 100 for 112 weeks, more than two years. By the end, most people had forgotten it was even still there. It hung on longer than “Heat Waves” and “Blinding Lights,” the two songs everyone jokes will never leave the charts. But here’s the strange part. While a handful of songs were sticking around for years, most were doing the exact opposite. Nearly half the songs that reached the chart showed up for a single week and then vanished for good.

Those two facts don’t sound like they belong together. They do. And together, they tell you the Hot 100 isn’t the chart it used to be.

For most of its history, hits big and small lived about the same length of life: a few months in the spotlight, then gone. That’s over. Look at every weekly Hot 100 from 1958 to 2025 and you can watch the typical song’s stay collapse, even as the biggest hits hang on longer than ever. The chart didn’t get faster or slower. It broke in two.

The chart below tracks two lines across the decades. One is the typical song, the middle of the pack. The other is the biggest hits, the top ten percent. For a long time they move as a pair. The story is in the moment they stop.

For fifty years, the two lines rose and fell together. The typical song peaked in 2001 and 2002, sticking around about 20 weeks, roughly five months. Then it fell off a cliff. Today the typical song is gone in two or three weeks. The biggest hits barely flinched. They have stayed up around 20 to 30 weeks since the ’90s. Back in 1995, a top hit lasted less than twice as long as an ordinary one. By 2021, it lasted about eleven times as long.

The averages tell you it happened. The next chart shows you. Every song is a single dot, placed by the year it charted and how long it lasted, and colored by year.

The split jumps out. The early years are a neat little band. After 2010 it tears open: a thick, growing cloud of songs that last a week or two, and a thin trail of giants climbing higher than anything before them. One-week songs were almost unheard of in the late ’70s and ’80s. By 2020 they were nearly half the chart. Meanwhile the songs that stuck around 20 weeks or more, more than half of all hits back in 2001, fell to about one in six. And the number of songs passing through the chart each year roughly doubled.

So what happened? Streaming, but it came in two waves. The first crack was downloads. Once iTunes made buying a single as easy as a click in the mid-2000s, people burned through songs faster, and one-week wonders started piling up. The bigger shift came when Billboard rebuilt the Hot 100 around streaming, adding on-demand plays in March 2012 and YouTube in February 2013. By 2016, streaming was simply how most of us listened.

Streaming pushed the chart in two directions at once. On one side is the “album bomb.” When a big artist drops a record, all of its songs flood the chart for a single week on a wave of streams, then disappear, a dozen one-week entries at a time. On the other side, a genuine smash can rack up weeks almost forever, because people keep hitting play month after month. What’s left is a chart with no middle. A song either blows up or blows away.

One honest caveat. The giants aren’t lasting longer purely because we love them more. Billboard has changed its own rules over the years for when an aging song gets bumped off the chart, so the chart itself now lets songs linger. (I’ve also left out this year, since those songs are still on the chart and their runs aren’t finished.)

Even so, the change is hard to miss. The slow-burn hit, the song a whole country falls for over a few months, is becoming a thing of the past. We used to share a handful of songs all season long. Now we share a few of them for what feels like forever, and the rest for about a weekend.
